passages.original: Noverat enim eodem spiritu, quo illi gentium praeconium credebatur, quod quando nationes credidissent, tunc periret domus Israel, et quod aliquando futurum erat, hoc ne in suo fieret tempore, verebatur. Unde imitatus Cain Jonas(Gen.IV), et recedens a facie Domini, fugere voluit in Tharsis, quam Josephus interpretatur Tharsum Ciliciae civitatem, prima 3 tamen littera commutata : quantum vero in Paralipomenon libris intelligi datur, quidam locus Indiae sic vocatur. Porro He- braei THARSIS (ΰΡΕΠΠ), mare dici generaliter autu- mant secundum illud : In spiritu vehementi con- fringes naves Tharsis (Psal.XLVII, 8), id est maris. Et in Isaia : Ululate, naves Tharsis (Isa.XXIII, 14). Super quo ante annos plurimos in epistola quadam ad Marcellam dixisse me memini : Non igitur propheta ad certum fugere cupiebat locum; sed mare ingrediens, quocunque pergere festinabat : et magis hoc convenit fugitivo et timido, non lo- cum fugae otiosae eligere, sed primam occasionem arripere navigandi.
passages.english: For he knew, by the same Spirit by which the preaching to the gentiles was being entrusted to him, that when the nations had believed, then the house of Israel would perish; and he feared that what was to happen at some time might happen in his own time. Hence Jonah imitated Cain (Gen. 4), and, departing from the face of the Lord, wanted to flee to Tarshish, which Josephus interprets as Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, though with the first letter changed; but as far as can be understood from the books of Chronicles, a certain place in India is so called. Further, the Hebrews hold that THARSIS means the sea in general, according to that [verse]: "With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish" (Ps. 47:8), that is, of the sea. And in Isaiah: "Howl, ships of Tarshish" (Isa. 23:14). On this matter I remember that many years ago I said in a certain letter to Marcella: "So the prophet did not desire to flee to a definite place, but, embarking on the sea, was hastening to go anywhere at all"; and this suits a fugitive and a frightened man better: not to choose a place for a leisurely flight, but to seize the first opportunity of sailing.
passages.notes: The Hebrew word in parentheses after THARSIS is garbled by the scan (ΰΡΕΠΠ) and is omitted. The stray "3" after "prima" is a footnote mark. Psalm numbering follows the Vulgate (Ps. 47 = Hebrew/English 48).

passages.original: Quid valeat apud homines saeculi eloquentia et sapientia saecularis, testes sunt Demosthenes, Tullius, Plato, Xenophon, Theophrastus, Aristoteles, et caeteri oratores ac phi- losophi, qui velut reges habentur hominum, et prae- cepta eorum non ut praecepta mortalium, sed quasi oracula accipiuntur deorum. Unde et Plato dicit : Felices fore respublicas, si aut philosophi regnent, aut reges philosophentur. 420 Quam autem difficile istiusmodi homines credant in Deum, ut quotidiana exempla praeteream, ct sileam de veteribus histo- riis ethnicorum, sufficit nobis Apostoli testimo- nium, qui ad Corinthios scribens, ait : Videte, fratres, vocationem vestram, quia non sunt multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes3, non multi nobiles : sed stulta mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes, et infirma mundi elegii Deus, ut confundat fortia, et ignobilia mundi, et ea quae erant contemptibilia elegit Deus (I Cor.I, 26–28). et caetera. Unde rursum dicit : Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et intelligentiam prudentium reprobabo (Ibid.
passages.english: What worldly eloquence and wisdom are worth among the people of this age is attested by Demosthenes, Tully, Plato, Xenophon, Theophrastus, Aristotle, and the other orators and philosophers, who are regarded as kings of men, and whose precepts are received not as the precepts of mortals but as if they were oracles of the gods. Hence Plato too says that states would be happy if either philosophers reigned or kings philosophized. But how hard it is for men of this kind to believe in God, to pass over everyday examples and say nothing of the ancient histories of the pagans, the testimony of the Apostle is enough for us, who, writing to the Corinthians, says: "Consider, brothers, your calling, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the base things of the world, and those that were contemptible, God chose" (1 Cor. 1:26–28), and so on. Hence again he says: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent" (ibid.
passages.notes: "Tully" is Cicero. The passage breaks off mid-reference; the context shows the citation continues as 1 Cor. 1:19.

passages.original: nemo bonus est nisi unus Deus (Marc.X, 18), Patrem interpretatus est bonum, 429 Filium vero ad comparationem ejus qui perfecte et vere bonus sit, in minori gradu positum. Et non con- sideravit haec dicens, quod in Marcionis potius, incurrerit haeresim (qui alterum Deum tantum bo- num, alterum infert judicem et conditorem) quam Arii, qui cum majorem Patrem et minorem Filium praedicet, tamen Filium non negat conditorem.
passages.english: "No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18), he interpreted the Father as the good one, but the Son as placed in a lesser rank by comparison with him who is perfectly and truly good. And in saying this he did not consider that he was falling into the heresy of Marcion (who introduces one God who is only good, and another who is judge and creator) rather than that of Arius, who, although he proclaims the Father greater and the Son lesser, nevertheless does not deny that the Son is the creator.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the subject ("he") is the unnamed interpreter mentioned in the preceding context, who took up the Gospel words "Why do you call me good?" The "429" in the text is a page or column number from the printed edition and has been omitted.
